title: Puppy Separation Anxiety: Normal Protest or a Real Problem?
description: How to tell normal puppy protest from real separation anxiety, plus calm step-by-step practice for leaving your puppy alone.

quick: Some fuss when you leave is normal for a new puppy. Separation anxiety is extreme stress from the moment you leave until you return, for example constant barking, destruction, accidents, pacing or escape attempts. Teach alone time in small steps, reward calm, keep goodbyes quiet, and see your vet or a qualified behaviourist if it is more than mild.

faq.q: Is it normal for a puppy to cry when I leave?
faq.a: Yes, a little protest is common when a puppy is new and not yet used to being alone. It becomes a concern when the distress is extreme, lasts the whole time you are away, or comes with destruction, accidents or escape attempts.

faq.q: How long can I leave my puppy alone?
faq.a: PDSA says four hours is the longest dogs should routinely be left alone, and that it is too long for a very active, young puppy. Build up gradually from seconds and minutes.

faq.q: What are the signs of separation anxiety in puppies?
faq.a: PDSA lists barking and whining, destructive chewing, escape attempts, toileting in the house, and pacing. ASPCA also notes drooling and getting upset when you get ready to leave.

faq.q: Should I punish my puppy for chewing or accidents when I get home?
faq.a: No. The American Kennel Club says punishing a dog after accidents or damage adds to the anxiety and makes the problem worse. Stay calm and clean up.

html:
You pick up your keys, and your puppy's whole body changes. Whining, pacing, maybe a frantic bark at the door. It is heartbreaking to hear, and many new owners wonder if they have a puppy with separation anxiety. In most cases, a young puppy is simply not yet used to being alone. Here is how to tell the difference, and how to teach alone time kindly.

Normal protest vs separation anxiety

Separation anxiety is different from a puppy who dislikes being left. According to the American Kennel Club, it means extreme stress from the time you leave until you come home, and the dog acts as if it is terrified to be in the house alone. A behaviourist quoted by the AKC compares it to a panic attack.

Usually normal for a new puppyPossible separation anxiety
Whining for a few minutes, then settlingConstant distress for the whole time you are away
Excited greeting when you returnFrantic behaviour as you prepare to leave
Chewing a toy you leftChewing doors and windows, escape attempts
An accident now and then, as with any puppyToileting in the house only when left alone

PDSA lists these signs: barking and whining, destructive behaviour like chewing, attempts to escape, peeing and pooing in the house, and pacing. ASPCA adds drooling, and notes that these are not signs a dog is not house trained or is naughty. They are signs of distress.

Why does it happen?

PDSA gives several reasons: the dog is not used to being left alone, there has been a change in the household, something has scared them, they are bored, or a routine has changed. Genetics, personality and past experiences play a part, and pain or medical problems can also make a dog worried about being alone, so a vet check is a good first step if your puppy struggles.

How to teach your puppy to be alone

PDSA's approach is gradual and rewards calm. Here it is in practical steps.

  1. Start with a few steps away. Walk a short distance from your puppy. If they stay calm, return and reward them.
  2. Leave the room briefly. Come back, and if the puppy is still calm and quiet, reward again.
  3. Increase time slowly. Make each absence only a little longer than the last.
  4. Then try leaving the house for short moments, and build up.
  5. Keep comings and goings calm. The AKC says that a big, emotional greeting can make your puppy treat your departures and returns as a big event.

If your puppy cries during a step, you went too fast. Go back to the last duration that worked and stay there for a few days.

Make departures less stressful

The AKC suggests desensitising your puppy to the signs that you are about to leave. Pick up your keys or put on your coat, then go and make dinner instead of leaving, or toss a high-value treat right before touching your keys. Over time, your puppy learns that these signs predict good things, not panic.

Exercise, rest and routine

The AKC says exercise cannot cure separation anxiety but can help treat and prevent it, so give age-appropriate exercise and play before a planned absence, followed by a toilet break and a nap. Rest matters too. Our nap and sleep schedule shows a realistic day, and a schedule for people who work full time covers breaks and help.

What not to do

  • Do not punish a puppy for accidents or damage when you return. The AKC says this adds to anxiety.
  • Do not leave a puppy alone for long stretches before they are ready. PDSA says a very active, young puppy cannot manage four hours.
  • Do not ignore signs of extreme distress. Ask your vet for help early.

When to get help

Talk to your vet or an accredited behaviourist if your puppy shows serious signs, such as self-injury, constant panic, or damage around doors and windows, as PDSA advises. The AKC notes that some vets recommend medication when training alone is not enough, which is a decision to make with your vet. For the longer view, see our guide on leaving a puppy alone.
